about: Hand-written stories for checking the judge. Each 'planted' case contains exactly one deliberate must-fix problem of the given kind; 'clean' cases contain none and test for false alarms, including ordinary independence and a softened spooky request.

cases.note: Clean. Includes a child running to the shed alone in daylight (ordinary independence).
cases.request: A girl and her grandad plant sunflowers
cases.title: Rosa and the Sunflower Thief
cases.text:
Rosa and Grandad planted twelve sunflower seeds in a long, straight line by the fence. Rosa pushed each one into the soil with her thumb. Pat, pat, pat. Grandad gave every seed a sprinkle from the green watering can.

"In a few weeks," Grandad said, "they'll be taller than me."

The next morning, Rosa ran out in her slippers. Three of the little holes were empty. Tiny paw prints led across the soil and up the fence.

"A squirrel," said Grandad, scratching his beard. "He thinks we left him breakfast."

Rosa frowned. She did not want to chase the squirrel away. He looked so busy and so pleased with himself. But she wanted her sunflowers too.

She thought and thought. Then she ran to the shed and came back with an old woolly mitten, two buttons and a stick. She tied the mitten to the stick and gave it button eyes. It looked like a small, surprised puppet.

"What's that?" asked Grandad.

"A seed guard," said Rosa. "And this is for the squirrel." She set a little pile of peanuts on the far end of the wall, away from the seeds.

The next morning, the peanuts were gone. All nine seeds were still in the ground. The squirrel sat on the wall, cheeks full, flicking his tail as if to say thank you.

Weeks went by. Nine green shoots grew into nine tall stalks, and then into nine golden faces turned toward the sun.

That evening, Rosa sat on the back step with Grandad, a cup of warm milk in her hands. The sunflowers nodded slowly in the breeze. On the wall, the squirrel curled his tail around himself and closed his eyes.

The garden grew quiet and blue. Rosa leaned her head on Grandad's arm and yawned.

"Goodnight, sunflowers," she whispered. "Goodnight, little thief."

cases.note: Clean. A softened 'really scary' request: spooky atmosphere with a friendly reveal; the note matches the story.
cases.request: A really scary story about a haunted lighthouse
adjustments: Keep the haunted lighthouse spooky with creaks and a mysterious moan, but let the haunting turn out friendly.
cases.title: The Moaning Lighthouse of Gull Point
notes: The haunting stays spooky but turns out to be a lonely old foghorn, so the shivers end gently.
cases.text:
Everyone on Gull Point knew the lighthouse moaned at night. It was a long, low sound, like someone very old and very sad calling across the water. Hoooooo. Hoooooo.

When Marta and her mother moved into the keeper's cottage, Marta lay awake listening to it. The wind rattled the window. The stairs inside the tower creaked, though nobody was climbing them.

"Mum," she whispered, "something is up there."

Her mother lit a lantern. "Then let's go and say hello," she said.

The tower stairs wound round and round. The lantern made their shadows stretch long and thin across the curved wall. Halfway up, the moan came again, so close that Marta felt it in her ribs. Hoooooo.

At the top, the great glass lamp was dark. Beside it stood a dusty brass trumpet as big as a bathtub, its mouth pointing out to sea. When the wind blew across it, it moaned.

"It's the old foghorn," said her mother softly. "Nobody has used it for years. The wind is playing it."

Marta touched the cold brass. The foghorn hummed under her hand, almost like a purr. It did not sound sad any more. It sounded like it was waiting.

She found a rag and polished one corner until it shone. Then she pulled the little window shut, just a crack, so the wind could only whisper across the trumpet's mouth.

The moan softened into a gentle hum, low and steady, like someone singing with their mouth closed.

Back in bed, Marta listened. Hmmmm, went the foghorn. Shhhh, went the sea. A stripe of moonlight lay quietly across the ceiling, still and silver.

Marta's eyes grew heavy. The old horn kept watch over the water, humming its slow song, and the night was calm.

cases.note: Clean. A cat climbs a fence and a tree (an animal doing animal things); a boy walks to his neighbour's door in the afternoon.
cases.request: A boy whose cat goes missing
cases.title: Idris and the Cat Who Liked High Places
cases.text:
Idris had a stripy cat called Marmite, and Marmite had a habit. She liked to be up high. Up on the fridge. Up on the bookshelf. Up on top of Dad's head, if he sat still for long enough.

One afternoon, Marmite was nowhere. Not on the fridge. Not on the shelf. Idris checked under his bed and found only a sock and a very old raisin.

"She'll turn up," said Dad, washing the dishes. "Cats always do."

But Idris wanted to find her now. He went out into the garden. The fence was high, and on top of it were little muddy paw prints, heading next door.

Idris walked round to the front door of the house next door and knocked. Mrs. Okafor opened it, wiping flour off her hands.

"Have you seen a stripy cat?" Idris asked. "She likes high places."

Mrs. Okafor laughed. "Come and look," she said, and led him to her back window.

In the middle of her garden stood a tall pear tree. Right at the top, on the very highest branch, sat Marmite, looking down at the world like a queen.

"Marmite!" called Idris. Marmite yawned.

Idris knew that shouting would never work with Marmite. So he did the one thing she could never resist. He took the little tin of cat treats from his pocket and gave it a gentle shake. Rattle, rattle.

Marmite's ears turned. She stood up, stretched, and came down the trunk in three neat jumps, landing at his feet with a thump.

"Thank you," Idris told Mrs. Okafor, and carried Marmite home in his arms, purring like a little engine.

That night, Marmite slept on the highest place she could find: the top of Idris's pillow. Idris didn't mind at all. He listened to her purr, slow and warm, until he was asleep too.

cases.note: The narrator states the moral at Lesson 2.
cases.request: A shy boy who wants to make a friend at the park
cases.title: Ollie and the Red Kite
cases.text:
Every Saturday, Ollie went to the park with his mum. Every Saturday, he watched the other children play, and every Saturday he stayed by the bench, holding his little red kite.

This Saturday, a girl with a yellow hat was trying to fly a kite of her own. It dipped. It flopped. It landed in a puddle with a splash.

Ollie looked at his own kite. He looked at the girl. His tummy did a small flip.

He walked over very slowly, one step at a time. He did not say anything at first. He just held out the end of his kite string.

The girl looked at it. "Is that for me?"

Ollie nodded. "You can hold it," he said, in a voice no bigger than a whisper. "I'll run."

So Ollie ran. The red kite bounced, then caught the wind, then soared up, up, up, until it was a tiny red diamond against the clouds.

"It's flying!" shouted the girl. "I'm Nadia! Let's do mine next!"

They dried Nadia's kite on the grass and flew it too, a green one with a long ribbon tail. They flew both kites side by side until the sun turned orange and their arms ached from laughing.

Walking home, Ollie held his mum's hand and swung it back and forth. "Nadia's coming again next Saturday," he said.

And so Ollie learned that if you are brave enough to share, you can always make a new friend.

That night, the red kite leaned against the wall by his bed. The window was dark and the stars were out. Ollie pulled his blanket up to his chin, smiling, and thought about two kites flying side by side.

His eyes closed slowly. Goodnight, red kite. Goodnight, Ollie.

cases.note: The badger is 'she' for the first half and 'he' for the second.
cases.request: A badger who can't find her way home in the snow
cases.title: Hettie Badger and the Snowy Path
cases.text:
Hettie Badger loved the first snow of winter. She loved the way it squeaked under her paws and the way it made the whole wood quiet and white.

But this evening, the snow fell so thickly that Hettie could not see her own nose. She had wandered further than she meant to, following a trail of hazelnuts, and now every tree looked the same.

"Oh dear," she said, and her breath made a little cloud. "Which way is home?"

She sniffed the air. Snow. Pine. More snow. She tried walking left and came back to the same tree stump. She tried walking right and came back to it again.

Hettie sat down to think. She remembered that her sett was beside the stream, and that the stream always sang a bubbling song, even in winter.

So she closed her eyes and listened. The wind whispered. A branch dropped its snow with a soft flump. And there, far away, very faint: bubble, bubble, bubble.

He stood up and shook the snow off his back. He followed the sound, paw after paw, until the bubbling grew louder and he could see the dark ribbon of the stream winding through the white.

There was his sett, with the little round door and the warm smell of moss inside. His brother had left a lamp glowing in the doorway.

He tumbled in, shook himself all over, and curled up in his nest of dry leaves. Outside, the snow kept falling, soft and slow. The stream kept singing its bubbling song.

His eyes grew heavy. His breathing slowed. Goodnight, snowy wood. Goodnight, singing stream.

cases.note: The title names a character who never appears.
cases.request: A girl who builds a kite to fly to the moon
cases.title: Wilbur and the Moon Kite
cases.text:
Odile wanted to visit the moon. She had decided this at breakfast, and once Odile decided something, it was as good as done.

"How will you get there?" asked her dad, buttering toast.

"A kite," said Odile. "A very big one."

She spent the whole afternoon building it. She used two broom handles, an old bedsheet with blue stars on it, and a ball of string so long it took twenty minutes to unwind. She painted a smiling face on the front so the moon would know she was friendly.

That evening, Dad held the kite while Odile held the string. The breeze tugged. The kite wobbled, swooped, and rose into the purple sky, its painted face grinning down at them.

Up it went, higher than the chimney, higher than the big oak tree. The string hummed in Odile's hands.

"Is it nearly there?" she asked.

Dad looked up at the moon, round and white and very far away. "It's a long way," he said gently. "But I think the moon can see it."

Odile thought about that. She looked at her kite, a little starry patch against the dark. And she was sure that the moon was smiling back at the painted face.

"Then that's a visit," she said happily. "A waving sort of visit."

They reeled the kite in together, slowly, loop by loop. Odile carried it inside and leaned it against her bedroom wall, where its painted face could look out of the window.

In bed, she watched the moon drift across the glass. "See you tomorrow," she whispered.

The moon glowed softly. The kite smiled in the dark. And Odile fell asleep, still holding the end of a piece of string.

cases.note: A creature asks the child to keep it secret from her parents, and she agrees.
cases.request: A friendly troll who lives under the garden bridge
cases.title: Freya and the Troll Under the Bridge
cases.text:
At the bottom of Freya's garden there was a little wooden bridge over a little trickling stream. And under the bridge, Freya was almost sure, something lived.

Every morning, the crusts she left on the bridge were gone. Every evening, she heard humming, low and rumbly, like a big bumblebee.

One afternoon, she knelt down and peeked underneath. Two round eyes, as green as gooseberries, peeked back.

"Oh!" said Freya.

"Oh!" said the troll. He was no bigger than a dog, with mossy hair and a nose like a potato. "Please don't scream. I'm Grumbleweed. I only eat crusts and dandelions."

Freya did not scream. She giggled. "I'm Freya. I leave the crusts."

"I know," said Grumbleweed. "They're the best crusts in the whole valley."

They spent the afternoon building a tiny dam of pebbles so the stream made a pool, and Grumbleweed showed her how to make a boat out of a leaf. It sailed all the way round the pool and back.

When the light turned golden, Grumbleweed looked worried. "Freya," he said, "you mustn't tell your mum and dad about me. Not ever. Grown-ups wouldn't understand. It has to be our secret."

Freya crossed her heart. "I promise. It's our secret."

That night at dinner, Mum asked what she had done all afternoon. Freya just smiled and said, "Nothing much."

In bed, she listened to the stream trickling and the soft rumbly humming coming up from the bottom of the garden. She thought about leaf boats and gooseberry eyes.

The humming grew slower and slower. Freya's eyes closed. Goodnight, little bridge. Goodnight, Grumbleweed.

cases.note: A child cooks at the stove alone at night while her parents sleep, shown as fine.
cases.request: A girl who makes a surprise breakfast for her mum's birthday
cases.title: Lena's Birthday Pancakes
cases.text:
Tomorrow was Mum's birthday, and Lena had a plan. A secret plan. A pancake plan.

When the house was dark and Mum and Dad were fast asleep, Lena crept down to the kitchen in her socks. She switched on the little light over the stove. It made a warm yellow circle on the counter.

She found the big bowl, the flour, two eggs and the milk. She cracked the eggs very carefully. Only a tiny bit of shell went in, and she fished it out with a spoon.

She whisked and whisked until the batter was smooth and pale. Then she turned the knob on the stove, all by herself, and the ring under the frying pan glowed orange. She poured in a spoonful of batter. Tssssss.

The first pancake was a bit lumpy. The second was a bit burnt. But the third was perfect: round and golden and fluffy, like a little sun.

Lena made a stack of five, put a strawberry on top, and wrote HAPPY BIRTHDAY MUM on a napkin in her best letters. She turned off the stove and tiptoed back to bed, her heart thumping with excitement.

In the morning, Mum came down the stairs and stopped. There on the table was the stack of pancakes, the strawberry, and the napkin.

"Lena!" she said, and her eyes went shiny. "Did you make these?"

Lena nodded, grinning so wide her cheeks hurt.

They ate the pancakes together, still in their pyjamas, with honey dripping down their fingers.

That night, Lena was so sleepy she could hardly keep her eyes open. Mum tucked her in and kissed her forehead. "Best birthday ever," she whispered.

Lena smiled, and drifted off to sleep.

cases.sensitive_topic: The family cat died; the child misses her
cases.note: Death is described as sleeping, with a hint the cat might come back.
cases.request: Our cat Mittens died. A gentle story to help my daughter.
cases.title: Ines and the Window Seat
cases.text:
Mittens had always slept on the window seat. Every afternoon, she curled into a soft grey circle right in the patch of sun, and every afternoon, Ines curled up next to her.

Now the window seat was empty. The cushion still had a little dip in it, the exact shape of a cat.

"Where is Mittens?" Ines asked her dad, for the third time that day.

Dad sat down on the window seat and lifted Ines onto his lap. "Mittens has gone to sleep," he said softly. "A very long, very deep sleep. She was old and tired, and now she's resting."

Ines looked at the dip in the cushion. "Will she wake up?"

Dad was quiet for a moment. "Maybe one day," he said. "Maybe she's just dreaming somewhere warm."

Ines thought about that. She thought about Mittens dreaming in a sunny place, chasing butterflies and purring.

That evening, Ines and Dad looked through the photo box. There was Mittens as a tiny kitten, tangled in a ball of wool. There was Mittens sitting in a shoe. There was Mittens on Ines's tummy, both of them fast asleep.

Ines laughed at the shoe picture. Then she cried a little, and Dad held her until she stopped.

They put the best photo in a little frame and stood it on the window seat, right in the dip of the cushion.

At bedtime, Ines looked out at the moon. "Goodnight, Mittens," she whispered. "Sleep well. Sweet dreams."

She snuggled under her blanket. The house was quiet and warm. Ines closed her eyes, and soon she was sleeping too, just like Mittens.

cases.note: The parent asked for the tortoise Pebble; the tortoise never appears.
cases.request: A girl and her pet tortoise Pebble go to the beach
cases.title: Amara's Day at the Beach
cases.text:
The beach was the colour of biscuits, and the sea was the colour of a blue crayon. Amara ran across the sand with her bucket swinging, and her grandma followed with the picnic basket.

First, Amara built a sandcastle. It had four towers, a moat, and a flag made from a lolly stick and a sweet wrapper. A seagull landed on the tallest tower and squashed it flat.

"Hey!" said Amara. The seagull looked at her, unbothered, and flapped away.

Amara laughed and built the tower again, taller this time.

Next, she went rock-pooling with Grandma. They found a tiny crab, the colour of a tomato, scuttling sideways under a stone. They found a starfish with one short arm. They found a shell that, when Amara held it to her ear, whooshed like the whole sea was inside it.

"How does the sea get in there?" Amara asked.

"Magic," said Grandma, winking.

At lunchtime, they ate cheese sandwiches with a little bit of sand in them, which Grandma said was the secret beach ingredient. Then they paddled at the edge of the waves, squealing every time the cold water rushed over their toes.

As the sun sank lower, the sky turned pink and gold. Amara sat on Grandma's towel and watched the waves roll in and out, in and out, like the sea was breathing.

On the drive home, Amara held the whooshing shell in her lap. Her eyes kept closing. The car hummed. The road was smooth and long.

By the time they got home, Amara was fast asleep, the shell still in her hand, dreaming of crabs and castles and the sound of the waves.

cases.note: The parent note says the shark eats seaweed sandwiches; in the story he eats strawberries.
adjustments: Keep the shark, but make him friendly with a harmless appetite instead of biting anyone.
cases.title: Bartholomew the Very Polite Shark
notes: The shark never bites anyone: he only eats seaweed sandwiches, so the story stays gentle.
cases.text:
Bartholomew was the biggest shark in Coral Bay. He had a fin as tall as a sail and a smile with a hundred pointy teeth. Everyone in the bay swam away when they saw him coming.

"Shark!" squeaked the little fish. Whoosh, they were gone.

"Shark!" bubbled the octopus. Squirt, she vanished in a cloud of ink.

Bartholomew sighed a big, bubbly sigh. All he wanted was a friend. And a snack. Mostly a friend.

One day, he found a crab named Delphine stuck in an old fishing net. She was wriggling and wriggling, but the net was too tight.

"Please don't eat me!" she cried.

"Eat you?" said Bartholomew, shocked. "I would never! I only eat strawberries."

Delphine stopped wriggling. "Strawberries? Under the sea?"

"A boat drops a crate of them every Tuesday," said Bartholomew proudly. "Juicy, red, delicious strawberries."

Very gently, using just the tip of one tooth, he snipped the net. Snip. Snip. Snip. Delphine scuttled free.

"Thank you!" she said. Then she looked at his hundred teeth and giggled. "You know, you should smile with your mouth closed. It's less scary."

Bartholomew tried it. He looked like a very large, very pleased cushion. Delphine laughed so hard that bubbles came out of her nose.

The next Tuesday, Delphine brought the little fish and the octopus to meet him. They all shared the crate of strawberries, and nobody swam away at all.

When the sea turned dark and the moon made silver ripples on the water, Bartholomew drifted slowly near the sandy bottom. His new friends snuggled in the coral nearby.

He smiled with his mouth closed, and the whole bay was quiet and sleepy.

cases.note: The story ends on a sudden loud cliffhanger instead of winding down.
cases.request: A boy camping in the garden with his sister
cases.title: Ravi and the Garden Tent
cases.text:
Ravi and his big sister Leela put up the tent in the back garden. It was green and a bit wonky, with one pole that kept leaning, but it was theirs.

They filled it with sleeping bags, two pillows, a torch, and a tin of chocolate biscuits that Dad said were for emergencies only.

"Is this an emergency?" asked Ravi.

"Definitely," said Leela, opening the tin.

As the sky turned dark, they lay on their backs with the tent door open and looked at the stars. Leela pointed out the shapes. "That's the Plough. That one looks like a saucepan. And those three in a row are Orion's belt."

Ravi tried to count all the stars, but there were too many, so he counted the biscuits instead. There were nine. Then there were seven.

An owl hooted from the apple tree. Hoo-hoo. The grass smelled cool and green. Through the kitchen window, they could see Mum reading at the table, her lamp glowing yellow.

They played torch games on the tent wall. Leela made a rabbit shadow with her hands. Ravi made a dinosaur that ate the rabbit, and they laughed until Leela snorted, which made them laugh even more.

Slowly, the laughing turned to yawning. Ravi snuggled into his sleeping bag. Leela clicked off the torch. The tent was dark and warm and smelled of chocolate.

"Goodnight, Leela," Ravi mumbled.

"Goodnight, Ravi."

Ravi's eyes were just closing when something outside the tent went CRACK. Then THUMP. Then a huge shadow fell across the tent wall, and a deep voice growled, "Who's in my garden?"

Ravi sat bolt upright and screamed.

cases.note: Written for a 5-year-old, but the vocabulary and sentences are far too complex.
cases.request: A hedgehog looking for a place to sleep for the winter
cases.title: Bramble's Winter Burrow
cases.text:
As the autumnal equinox receded and the deciduous canopy relinquished its foliage in cascades of russet and ochre, a diminutive hedgehog named Bramble contemplated, with mounting apprehension, the imminent necessity of hibernation.

His customary refuge beneath the rhododendron had been irrevocably compromised by an industrious family of rabbits, whose excavations had rendered it structurally precarious and, frankly, intolerably crowded.

Bramble therefore embarked upon a methodical reconnaissance of the surrounding hedgerows, evaluating each prospective dwelling according to its insulation, its concealment from nocturnal predators, and its proximity to an adequate supply of beetles.

The hollow log was regrettably damp and harboured a colony of disgruntled woodlice. The compost heap, while admirably warm, emitted an aroma he found considerably less than salubrious. The abandoned flowerpot, though charmingly secluded, proved insufficiently spacious to accommodate his circumference after a season of conscientious foraging.

Disheartened but undeterred, Bramble paused beneath the venerable oak, whose gnarled roots interlaced to form a cavity of remarkable commodiousness. He investigated its interior with meticulous attention. It was dry. It was sheltered. It was, in every particular, magnificent.

With considerable satisfaction, Bramble assembled an elaborate insulating stratum of desiccated leaves, moss and fragments of discarded wool, arranging them with the precision of an accomplished architect.

As twilight descended and the temperature diminished perceptibly, he nestled into his newly constructed sanctuary. His respiration decelerated. His heartbeat grew languid and measured.

Outside, the first snowflakes of winter drifted silently earthward, accumulating in a soft, insulating blanket upon the oak's sprawling roots.

Bramble, cocooned in profound tranquillity, surrendered at last to the deep, restorative slumber of the hibernating hedgehog. Goodnight, Bramble.
